title: Epistulae
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa011.opp-lat2, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: nec tam stultus sum, ut diuersitate explanationum tuarum me laedi putem, quia nec tu laederis, si nos contraria senserimus. sed illa est uera inter amicos reprehensio, si nostram peram non uidentes aliorum iuxta Persium manticam consideremus. superest, ut diligas diligentem et in scripturarum campo iuuenis senem non prouoces. nos nostra habuimus tempora et cucurrimus, quantum potuimus. nunc te currente et longa spatia transmittente nobis debetur otium simulque, ut cum uenia et honore tuo dixerim, ne solus mihi de poetis aliquid proposuisse uidearis, memento Daretis et Entelli et uulgaris prouerbii, quod bos lassus fortius figat pedem.
passages.english: Nor am I so foolish as to think myself injured by the difference of your interpretations, since you are not injured either if we have held contrary views. But that is true reproach among friends, if, not seeing our own wallet, we look at the knapsack of others, as Persius says. It remains that you love one who loves you, and that in the field of the Scriptures you, a young man, do not challenge an old one. We have had our times, and we have run as far as we could. Now, while you are running and covering long distances, rest is owed to us; and at the same time, if I may say it with your leave and with respect to you, so that you may not seem to be the only one to have put forward something to me from the poets, remember Dares and Entellus, and the common proverb that a tired ox plants its foot more firmly.
passages.notes: This letter is by Jerome, written to Augustine, and preserved among Augustine's letters. The proverb of 'our wallet' and 'others' knapsack' is attributed to Persius (Satires 4.24). Dares and Entellus are the boxers in Virgil, Aeneid 5.

passages.original: Hanc autem expositionem, quam primus Origenes in decimo Stromatum libro, ubi epistulam Pauli ad Galatas interpretatur, et ceteri deinceps interpretes sunt secuti, illa uel maxime causa subintroducunt, ut Porphyrio respondeant blasphemanti, qui Pauli arguit procacitatem, quod principem apostolorum Petrum ausus sit reprehendere et arguere in faciem ac ratione constringere, quod male fecerit, id est in eo errore fuerit, in quo fuit ipse, qui alium arguit delinquentem.
passages.english: Now this explanation, which Origen first [gave] in the tenth book of the Stromateis, where he interprets Paul's letter to the Galatians, and which the other interpreters have followed in turn, they introduce above all for this reason: to answer the blasphemer Porphyry, who charges Paul with impudence, because he dared to rebuke the prince of the apostles, Peter, and to reprove him to his face and bind him by argument for having acted wrongly, that is, for having been in the same error in which he himself was, who reproved another for doing wrong.
passages.notes: The speaker is Jerome (letter to Augustine). The final clause is condensed. It seems to mean that Porphyry's charge is that Paul shared the very fault for which he rebuked Peter.

passages.original: non enim propter malos boni deserendi, sed propter bonos mali tolerandi sunt, sicut tolerarunt prophetae, contra quos tanta dicebant, nec communionem sacramentorum illius populi relinquebant, sicut ipse dominus nocentem ludam usque ad condignum eius exitum tolerauit et eum sacram cenam cum innocentibus communicare permisit, sicut tolerarunt apostoli eos, qui per inuidiam, quod ipsius diaboli uitium est, Christum adnuntiabant, sicut tolerauit Cyprianus collegarum auaritiam, quam secundum apostolum appellat idolatriam. postremo quicquid tunc inter illos episcopos gestum est, etiam si forte ab aliquibus eorum sciebatur, si non sit acceptio personarum, nunc ab omnibus ignoratur. cur ergo non ab omnibus pax amatur?\' haec facillime cogitare possetis aut fortasse etiam cogitatis.
passages.english: For the good are not to be deserted on account of the bad; rather, the bad are to be tolerated on account of the good. So the prophets tolerated [them], though they said so much against them, and they did not abandon communion in the sacraments of that people. So the Lord himself tolerated the guilty Judas until his fitting end, and allowed him to share the sacred supper with the innocent. So the apostles tolerated those who proclaimed Christ out of envy, which is the vice of the devil himself. So Cyprian tolerated the avarice of his colleagues, which, following the apostle, he calls idolatry. Finally, whatever was done at that time among those bishops, even if perhaps it was known by some of them, is now unknown to all, if there is no respect of persons. Why then is peace not loved by all?' You could very easily think these things, or perhaps you even do think them.
passages.notes: 'ludam' is read as 'Iudam' (Judas). The closing quotation mark implies that a quoted speech ends here, but the passage contains no opening mark.

passages.original: tu autem non bonum facis, ut timere non debeas potestatem, nisi forte bonum est sedere et non aduersus fratrem detrahere sed aduersus fratres omnes in omnibus gentibus constitutos. quibus testimonium perhibent prophetae, Christus, apostoli, cum legitur: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes, cum legitur: Ab ortu solis usque ad occasum sacrificium mundum offertur nominimeo, quoniam glorificatum est nomen meum in gentibus, dicit dominus — audi: \'dicit dominus\', non: dicit Donatus aut Rogatus aut Vincentius aut Hilarius aut Ambrosius aut Augustinus sed: \'dicit dominus\' —, cum legitur: Et benedicentur in eo omnes tribus terrae, omnes gentes magnificabunt eum. benedictus dominus deus Israhel, qui facit mirabilia solus, et benedictum nomen gloriae eius in aeternum et in saeculum saeculi. et replebitur gloria eius omnis terra. fiat, fiat. et tu sedes Cartennis et cum decem Rogatistis, qui remansistis, dicis: (Non fiat, non fiat).
passages.english: But you are not doing good, so that you need not fear the authority, unless perhaps it is good to sit and speak against, not a brother, but all the brothers established in all nations. To them the prophets, Christ and the apostles bear witness, when it is read: 'In your seed all nations shall be blessed'; when it is read: 'From the rising of the sun to its setting a pure sacrifice is offered to my name, because my name has been glorified among the nations, says the Lord.' Listen: 'says the Lord', not 'says Donatus', or Rogatus, or Vincentius, or Hilary, or Ambrose, or Augustine, but 'says the Lord'. And when it is read: 'And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders, and blessed be the name of his glory for ever and for ages of ages. And the whole earth shall be filled with his glory. So be it, so be it.' And you sit at Cartenna, and with the ten Rogatists who are left, you say: 'Let it not be, let it not be.'
passages.notes: 'nominimeo' is read as 'nomini meo'.

passages.original: Tale tunc erat tempus, de quo scripsit Hilarius, unde putasti insidiandum contra testimonia tot diuina, tamquam perierit ecclesia de orbe terrarum. potes hoc modo dicere nec tot ecclesias Galatiae tunc fuisse, quando dicebat apostolus: s o stulti Galatae, quis uos fascinauit? et: Cum spiritu coeperitis, nunc carne consummamini? sic enim calumniaris docto uiro, qui tardicordes et timidos grauiter increpabat, quos iterum parturiebat, donec Christus formaretur in eis.
passages.english: Such was the time then, about which Hilary wrote, from which you thought you should lay an ambush against so many divine testimonies, as if the Church had perished from the world. In this way you could say that there were not so many churches of Galatia at the time when the apostle said: 'O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?' and: 'Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being completed in the flesh?' For in this way you slander a learned man, who was sharply rebuking the slow of heart and the timid, with whom he was again in labour until Christ should be formed in them.
passages.notes: The stray 's' before 'o stulti' is treated as a footnote mark and left out. The sense of 'potes hoc modo dicere nec...fuisse' is that by the same reasoning one could deny that the Galatian churches existed.

passages.original: Noli ergo, frater, contra diuina tam multa, tam clara, tam indubitata testimonia colligere uelle calumnias ex episcoporum scriptis siue nostrorum sicut Hilarii siue, antequam pars Donati separaretur, ipsius unitatis sicut Cypriani et Agrippini primo, quia hoc genus litterarum ab auctoritate canonis distinguendum est. non enim sic leguntur, tamquam ita ei eis testimonium proferatur, ut contra sentire non liceat, sicubi fOl\'te aliter sapuerunt, quam ueritas postulat.
passages.english: Do not, then, brother, seek to gather slanders against so many divine testimonies, so clear and so beyond doubt, from the writings of bishops. [These are] either ours, such as Hilary, or [those] of the unity itself before the party of Donatus was separated, such as Cyprian and Agrippinus. [Do not], first, because this kind of writing must be distinguished from the authority of the canon. For they are not read as though testimony were brought from them in such a way that it is not permitted to think otherwise, wherever perhaps they held views other than the truth demands.
passages.notes: 'ei eis' is read as 'ex eis'. 'fOl\'te' is read as 'forte'.

passages.original: Qua in re, sicut ingenium tuum noui, facillime perspicis totam causam uestram penitus euersam et extinctam. si enim sacramenta cum peccatoribus communicando, sicut putatis, periit ecclesia, quae fuerat in orbe terrarum — nam uos ideo separastis —, iam prius tota perierat, cum, sicut dicit Cyprianus, in eam sine baptismo admittebantur, ac sic nec ipse Cyprianus habebat, in qua ecclesia nasceretur, quanto magis multo posterior uester auctor paterque Donatus! si autem illo tempore, cum in eam sine baptismo admittebantur.
passages.english: In this matter, as I know your intelligence, you very easily see that your whole case is utterly overturned and extinguished. For if the Church that had been throughout the world perished by sharing the sacraments with sinners, as you think (for that is why you separated), then it had already perished entirely before, when, as Cyprian says, people were admitted into it without baptism. And so not even Cyprian himself had a church in which to be born, much less your far later founder and father Donatus! But if at that time, when people were admitted into it without baptism,
passages.notes: The final sentence is incomplete. It continues in the following context, where the full stop after 'admittebantur' appears to be an editorial or scanning error.

passages.original: nam in illis quidem interfectionem non faciunt, sed, quantum in ipsis est, interfectores fiunt. recte illis dicitur, quando ab hoc scelere prohibentur: \'Nolite occidere paruulos uestros\', dicit enim et apostolus: Spiritum nolite extinguere, non quia ille extingui potest, sed, quantum in ipsis est, extinctores eius merito dicuntur, qui sic agunt, ut extinctum uelint. isto sensu recte intellegi potest, quod scripsit beatissimus Cyprianus in epistula de lapsis, cum eos, qui tempore persecutionis idolis immolauerant, arguens: (Ac ne quid deesset\', inquit, (ad criminis cumulum, infantes quoque parentum manibus inpositi uel adtracti amiserunt paruuli quod in primo statim natiuitatis exordio fuerant consecuti\'. amiserunt, dixit, quantum adtinuit ad illorum scelus, a quibus amittere coacti sunt; amiserunt in eorum mente ac uoluntate, qui in illos tantum facinus commiserunt;
passages.english: For in their case they do not commit killing, but, as far as lies in them, they become killers. It is rightly said to them, when they are prevented from this crime: 'Do not kill your little ones.' For the apostle too says: 'Do not extinguish the Spirit.' This is not because he can be extinguished; but those who act so as to wish him extinguished are deservedly called his extinguishers, as far as lies in them. In this sense one can rightly understand what the most blessed Cyprian wrote in his letter on the lapsed, when, rebuking those who had sacrificed to idols in the time of persecution, he says: 'And so that nothing might be lacking to the heap of the crime, infants too, placed in or dragged by their parents' hands, lost as little ones what they had obtained at the very first beginning of their birth.' 'They lost,' he said, as far as concerned the crime of those by whom they were forced to lose [it]. They lost in the mind and will of those who committed so great a wrong against them;

passages.original: nuoniam uita ipsa, qua fruimur, breuis est, in qua tu arbitraris et frequentatum in litteris iam mones aeternam esse posse calamitatem; mortem autem malorum omnium esse finem habent quidem uestrae litterae sed nec ipsae omnes; Epicureorum est quippe ista sententia et si qui alii mortalem animam putant. at illi, quos Tullius quasi consulares philosophos\' appellat, quod eorum magni pendat auctoritatem, quoniam, cum extremum diem fungimur, non extingui animam sed emigrare censent, et ut merita quoque eius adserunt seu bona seu mala uel ad beatitudinem uel ad miseriam permanere.
passages.english: Since the very life we enjoy is short, in which you think, and as is often said in [your] literature you now remind [me], that calamity can be eternal: your literature does indeed hold that death is the end of all evils, but not all of it does. That opinion belongs to the Epicureans, and to any others who think the soul mortal. But those whom Tully calls 'consular philosophers', because he values their authority highly, hold that when we reach our last day the soul is not extinguished but departs, and they also assert that its merits, whether good or bad, remain, leading either to blessedness or to misery.
passages.notes: 'nuoniam' is read as 'quoniam'. The first sentence is syntactically confused, probably through corruption, and the rendering is tentative. 'Tully' is Cicero. 'cum extremum diem fungimur' is taken as 'when we reach our last day'.

passages.original: non tunc benefici sumus, cum id, quod a nobis petitur, facimus, sed cum id facimus, quod non obsit petentibus. nam pleraque non dando prosumus et noceremus, si dedissemus. unde illud prouerbium: Nec puero gladium. (Tu uero\', inquit Tullius, \'ne unico quidem filio\'. quo enim quemquam maxime diligimus, eo minus ei debemus, in quibus magno periculo peccatur, committere. et de diuitiis, ni fallor, cum haec ageret, loquebatur. proinde quae periculose male utentibus committuntur, salubriter etiam plerumque detrahuntur.
passages.english: We are not kind when we do what is asked of us, but when we do what does not harm those who ask. For in many cases we help by not giving, and we would harm if we had given. Hence that proverb: 'Do not [give] a boy a sword.' 'Nor indeed,' says Tully, 'to an only son.' For the more we love someone, the less we ought to entrust to him those things in which one goes wrong at great risk. And he was speaking, unless I am mistaken, about riches when he was treating these matters. Accordingly, things that are entrusted with danger to those who use them badly are also, for the most part, taken away to their benefit.
passages.notes: 'Tully' is Cicero.

passages.original: Istam caritatis legem ex ore Christi domini promulgatam — ipsius enim sunt istae similitudines et de zizaniis usque ad tempus messis in unitate agri per mundum et de malis piscibus usque ad tempus litoris intra eadem retia tolerandis hanc ergo caritatis legem si maiores uestri mente retinerent, si cum dei timore cogitarent non propter Caecilianum et nescio quos Afros siue, ut putatis, re uera criminosos siue, quod magis credendum est, calumniis appetitos se ab ecclesia, quam descripsit ipse Cyprianus per omnes gentes radios suos porrigere et ramos suos per omnem terram copia ubertatis extendere, non, inquam, se a tot gentibus Christianis, quae omnino nescierunt, qui uel quid uel quibus obiciebant, nefaria separatione discinderent, quod non fit nisi aut simultate priuata potius quam utilitate communi aut illo uitio, quod consequenter Cyprianus ipse conumerat uitandumque commemorat. nam cum praecepisset propter zizania, quae in ecclesia cernuntur, non esse ecclesiam deserendam, sequitur et adiungit: \'Nobis tantum modo laborandum est, ut frumentum esse possimus, ut. cum coeperit frumentum dominicis horreis condi, fructum pro opere nostro et labore capiamus. apostolus in epistula sua dicit: In domo autem magna non solum sunt uasa aurea et argentea sed et lignea et fictilia et quaedam quidem honorata quaedam inhonorata. nos operam demus et, quantum possumus, laboremus, ut uas aureum et argenteum simus. ceterum fictilia uasa confringere domino soli licitum est, cui et uirga ferrea data est.
passages.english: This law of charity, promulgated from the mouth of Christ the Lord (for these similitudes are his, both of the tares that are to be tolerated in the unity of the field throughout the world until the time of harvest, and of the bad fish that are to be tolerated within the same nets until the time of reaching the shore), this law of charity, then, if your forefathers had kept it in mind, if they had reflected with the fear of God, they would not, on account of Caecilian and some Africans or other, whether, as you think, truly criminal, or, as is more to be believed, assailed by slanders, have torn themselves by a wicked separation from the Church, which Cyprian himself described as stretching out its rays through all nations and extending its branches through the whole earth with abundance of fruitfulness; they would not, I say, have torn themselves away from so many Christian nations, which had no idea at all who was accusing, or of what, or whom. This does not happen except either through private rivalry rather than the common good, or through that vice which Cyprian himself goes on to list and warns must be avoided. For when he had taught that the Church must not be abandoned on account of the tares that are seen in the Church, he follows and adds: 'We must labour only that we may be wheat, so that, when the wheat begins to be stored in the Lord's barns, we may receive fruit for our work and labour. The apostle says in his letter: But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of earthenware, and some honoured, some dishonoured. Let us take pains and labour as much as we can, that we may be a vessel of gold and silver. But to break the earthenware vessels is permitted to the Lord alone, to whom also a rod of iron has been given.
passages.notes: The opening sentence is anacoluthic in the Latin (the object 'this law of charity' is resumed after the parenthesis); rendered accordingly. The quotation from Cyprian continues beyond the passage.

passages.original: Deinde si fallor et quisquam ibi forte huius modi quaestionum tanto utique odiosior quanto in illis locis ineptior percontator extiterit, nonne magis caues, ne multo facilius existant, qui te Graeci homines in Graecia constitutum et Graeca inbutum primitus lingua de ipsis philosophorum libris aliqua interrogent, quae Cicero in suis litteris non posuit? quod si acciderit, quid responsurus es? potius te ista in Latinorum auctorum libris quam in Graecorum nosse uoluisse? qua responsione primo Graeciae facies iniuriam et nosti, quam illi homines hoc non ferant;
passages.english: Next, if I am mistaken and someone there should perhaps turn up as a questioner about questions of this kind, all the more odious the more out of place he is in those parts, are you not rather on your guard lest there should much more easily appear Greek men who question you, settled in Greece and steeped from the first in the Greek language, about things from the very books of the philosophers which Cicero did not put in his writings? If that happens, what will you answer? That you preferred to know these things from the books of Latin authors rather than of Greek ones? By that answer you will first do an injury to Greece, and you know how those men do not put up with this;

passages.original: Item Anaxagoras siue quilibet si mentem dicit ipsam ueritatem atque sapientiam, quid mihi est de uerbo cum homine contendere? manifestum est enim omnium rerum descriptionem et modum ab illa fieri eamque non incongrue dici infinitam non per spatia locorum sed per potentiam, quae cogitatione humana comprehendi non potest, neque quod informe aliquid sit ipsa sapientia;
passages.english: Likewise, if Anaxagoras, or anyone else, calls mind truth itself and wisdom, why should I quarrel with the man about a word? For it is evident that the ordering and measure of all things comes about from it, and that it is not inappropriately called infinite, not through extension in space but through power, which cannot be grasped by human thought; nor [is it called infinite] because wisdom itself is something formless;

passages.original: sed adiungit: \'Quid autem interius mente?\' non ergo potest mens habere interiorem animam, ut sit animal, quia ipsa est interior. ergo corpus habeat extrinsecus, cui sit interior, ut sit animal!. hoc est enim, quod ait: \'Cingatur igitur corpore externo\', quasi Anaxagoras dixerit, nisi animalis alicuius esset, mentem esse non posse, si mentem ipsam summam sapientiam esse sentiebat, quae nullius quasi animantis propria est, quia omnibus animis se frai ualentibus ueritas communiter praesto est.
passages.english: But he adds: 'And what is more inward than mind?' Therefore mind cannot have a soul more inward than itself, so as to be a living being, because it is itself the inward thing. So then let it have a body on the outside, to which it may be inward, so that it may be a living being! For this is what he says: 'Let it then be surrounded by an external body', as if Anaxagoras had said that mind could not exist unless it belonged to some living being, when he held that mind itself was the highest wisdom, which is the property of no living being, as it were, because truth is available in common to all souls that are able to enjoy it.
passages.notes: 'frai' read as 'frui' (enjoy); 'animal!' taken as a scanning artefact for 'animal'.

passages.original: Quamquam Democritus etiam hoc distare in naturalibus quaestionibus ab Epicuro dicitur, quod iste sentit inesse concursioni atomorum uim quandam animalem et spirabilem, qua ui eum credo et (imagines) ipsas diuinitate praeditas) dicere, non omnes omnium rerum sed deorum, et \'principia mentis\' esse (in uniuerso\', quibus diuinitatem tribuit, et \'animantes imagines, quae uel prodesse nobis soleant uel nocere\'.
passages.english: Although Democritus is also said to differ from Epicurus in questions of natural philosophy in this, that he holds that there is in the concourse of atoms a certain animate and breathing force; by this force, I believe, he also says that the images themselves are endowed with divinity (not all the images of all things, but those of the gods), and that there are 'principles of mind' in the universe, to which he attributes divinity, and 'living images, which are accustomed either to benefit or to harm us'.
passages.notes: The edition's brackets and quotation marks are garbled by scanning; the sense is clear.

passages.original: quo modo igitur totae simul cogitantur, si in tantum cogitantur, in quantum uenientes atque intrantes animum adtingunt, quae nec totae intrare possunt per tam paruum corpus nec totae tam paruum animum ? adtingere? memento me secundum illos haec dicere — non enim ego talem animum sentio — aut, si incorporeum Democritus animum existimat, Epicurus quidem solus ista ratione urgeri potest; sed etiam ille quare non uidit non opus esse nec fieri posse, ut incorporeus animus aduentu atque contactu corporearum imaginum cogitet? de uisu certe oculorum ambo pariter redarguuntur;
passages.english: How, then, are they thought of whole all at once, if they are thought of only to the extent that, coming and entering, they touch the mind, when they can neither enter whole through so small a body nor touch whole so small a mind? Remember that I am saying these things according to their view (for I do not perceive the mind to be such), or, if Democritus considers the mind incorporeal, Epicurus alone can indeed be pressed by this argument; but why did even Democritus not see that it is neither necessary nor possible for an incorporeal mind to think by the arrival and contact of corporeal images? Concerning the sight of the eyes, certainly, both are refuted equally;

passages.original: quod ergo ad magisterium eius adtinet, quis nunc extremus idiota uel quae abiecta muliercula non credit animae inmortalitatem uitamque post mortem futuram? quod apud Graecos olim primus Pherecydes Syrius cum disputauisset, Pythagoram Samium disputationis illius nouitate permotum ex athleta in philosophum uertit. nunc ergo, quod Maro ait et omnes uidemus, amomum Assyrium uulgo nascitur. quod autem ad adiutorium gratiae pertinet, quae in Christo est, ipse est omnino, quo duce, si qua manent sceleris uestigia nostri,inrita perpetua soluent formidine terras.
passages.english: As for what concerns his teaching, then, what utter simpleton or what lowly little woman does not now believe in the immortality of the soul and a life to come after death? When Pherecydes the Syrian first argued this long ago among the Greeks, he turned Pythagoras of Samos, stirred by the novelty of that argument, from an athlete into a philosopher. Now, therefore, as Maro says and we all see, Assyrian amomum grows everywhere. As for what pertains to the help of grace, which is in Christ, he himself is altogether the one under whose leadership, 'if any traces of our wickedness remain, made void, they will free the lands from perpetual fear.'
passages.notes: Quotations from Virgil (Maro), Eclogue 4.

passages.original: unde quid opus est, ut diutius laboremus ac non ipsos potius percontemur, quo modo poterant gubernare atque augere rem publicam, quam ex parua et inopi magnam opulentamque fecerunt, qui \'accepta iniuria ignoscere quam persequi malebant\'? quo modo Caesari, utique administratori rei publicae, mores eius extollens Cicero dicebat, quod nihil obliuisci soleret nisi iniurias? dicebat enim hoc tam magnus laudator aut tam magnus adulator; sed si laudator, talem Caesarem nouerat, si autem adulator, talem esse debere ostendebat principem ciuitatis, qualem illum fallaciter praedicabat.
passages.english: Why then do we need to labour longer, and not rather ask these men themselves how they were able to govern and enlarge the commonwealth, which they made great and wealthy out of small and poor, men who 'when they had received an injury preferred to pardon rather than pursue it'? How was it that Cicero, extolling the character of Caesar, certainly an administrator of the commonwealth, said that he was accustomed to forget nothing except injuries? For so great a praiser, or so great a flatterer, said this; but if a praiser, he knew Caesar to be such; if a flatterer, he showed that the leading man of the state ought to be such as he falsely proclaimed Caesar to be.

passages.original: sed si in bonam partem accipiatur, ut quempiam talem fuisse credamus, qui cum sapienter omnia loqueretur, nullum umquam uerbum, quod reuocare uellet, emisit, hoc potius de hominibus dei, qui spiritu sancto acti locuti sunt, quam de illo, quem sic Cicero laudat, saluberrima pietate credendum est. ab hac ego excellentia tam longe absum, ut, si nullum uerbum, quod reuocare uellem, protulero, fatuo sim quam sapienti similior. illius quippe scripta summa sunt auctoritate dignissima, qui nullum uerbum, non quod reuocare uellet.
passages.english: But if it is taken in a good sense, so that we believe someone was such that, since he spoke everything wisely, he never let slip a single word he would wish to recall, this is to be believed, with most wholesome piety, of the men of God who spoke moved by the Holy Spirit rather than of the man whom Cicero praises in this way. I am so far from this excellence that, if I have uttered no word I would wish to recall, I would be more like a fool than a wise man. For the writings of that man are most worthy of the highest authority who let slip no word, not that he would wish to recall,
passages.notes: The sentence runs on into the following context ('but which he ought to recall').

passages.original: (nidi t) enim ad utrumque referendum est\', restat inquirere, quo modo angeli deum uideant, propter illud, quod ex euangelio commemoraui: Angeli eorum semper uident faciem patris mei. si enim et ipsis non sicuti est, sed latente sua natura in specie, qua uoluerit, apparet, magis magisque requirendum est, quo modo eum nos uidebimus, sicuti est et sicut Moyses desiderauit, cum peteret, ut deus, qui in conspectu eius erat, ostenderet illi semet ipsum. hoc enim nobis summum praemium in resun-ectione promittitur, quod erimus aequales angelis dei, ac per hoc, si nec ipsi eum uident, sicuti est, quo modo nos ita uisuri sumus, cum eis aequales in resurrectione facti fuerimus? sed uide, quid consequenter dicat noster Ambrosius: \'Denique\', inquit, (cum additur: Unigenitus filius ipse narrauit, mentium magis quam oculorum uisio declaratur. species enim uidetur, uirtus uero narratur; illa oculis, haec mente comprehenditur\'. qui paulo ante dixerat uisionem ad utrumque referendam, nunc eam non menti sed oculis dedit non, ut opinor, neglegenter sua uerba respiciens, sed quia usitatius in loquendo solemus oculis adtribuere uisionem sicut speciem corpori.
passages.english: 'For [vision] is to be referred to both', it remains to inquire how the angels see God, on account of what I cited from the Gospel: Their angels always see the face of my Father. For if to them too he appears not as he is, but with his nature hidden, in whatever form he wishes, it must be inquired more and more how we shall see him as he is, and as Moses desired when he asked that God, who was in his sight, would show himself to him. For this is promised to us as the highest reward in the resurrection, that we shall be equal to the angels of God; and therefore, if not even they see him as he is, how are we to see him so when we have been made equal to them in the resurrection? But see what our Ambrose says next: 'Finally,' he says, 'when it is added: The only-begotten Son himself has declared [him], a vision of minds rather than of eyes is made known. For a form is seen, but power is declared; the one is grasped by the eyes, the other by the mind.' He who had said a little before that vision is to be referred to both now assigned it not to the mind but to the eyes, not, I think, through carelessly regarding his own words, but because in speaking we more commonly attribute vision to the eyes, just as form to the body.
passages.notes: The opening '(nidi t)' is a scanning corruption, probably of 'uisio' or similar; the sentence continues from the preceding context ('... since ... vision is to be referred to both').

passages.original: Quod ergo ait sanctus Ambrosius \'neque is, qui deum uidere noluerit, potest deum uidere\\ quid aliud intellegi uoluit, nisi quia is, qui mundando cordi curam tanta re dignam non uult inpendere, non uult deum uidere? uide proinde, quid adiungat: \'Nec in loco\', inquit, \'deus uidetur sed mundo corde\\ quid euidentius, quid expressius dici potuit?
passages.english: When, then, Saint Ambrose says, 'nor can he who has not wished to see God see God', what else did he wish to be understood than that he who does not wish to spend on cleansing the heart the care worthy of so great a thing does not wish to see God? See, accordingly, what he adds: 'Nor is God seen in a place,' he says, 'but by a pure heart.' What could be said more clearly, more expressly?

passages.original: tunc quippe satiabitur in bonis desiderium eorum, quo desiderio flagrabat Moyses, cui loqui ad deum facie ad faciem non sufficiebat et dicebat: Ostende mihi temet ipsum manifeste, ut uideam te, tamquam diceret, quod in psalmo ex eodem desiderio canitur: Satiabor, cum manifestabitur gloria tua; quo desiderio ardebat et Philippus et sic satiari cupiebat dicens: Ostende nobis patrem et sufficit nobis. de hac uisione loquens eius etiam ipse amator et desiderator Ambrosius: \'Non in loco.., inquit, \'deus uidetur* sicut ad ilicem Mambre, sicut in monte Sina (sed mundo corde\'; et sequitur sciens, quid desideret et quid aestuet et quid speret: \'Nec corporalibus\', inquit, \'oculis deus quaeritur\\ quibus se ostendit Abrahae, Isaac, Iacob et aliis in hoc saeculo, \'nec circumscribitur uisu propter illud, quod dictum est: Posteriora mea uidebis, \'nec tactu tenetur\', sicut etiam luctatus est cum Iacob, (nec auditur affatu\', sicut non solum a tot sanctis uerum etiam a diabolo auditus est, (nec sentitur incessu* sicut aliquando, cum in paradiso deambularet ad uesperam.
passages.english: For then their desire will be satisfied with good things, the desire with which Moses burned, for whom speaking with God face to face was not enough, and who said: Show me yourself plainly, that I may see you, as if he were saying what is sung in the psalm from the same desire: I shall be satisfied when your glory is made manifest; the desire with which Philip too was on fire and longed to be satisfied in this way, saying: Show us the Father and it is enough for us. Speaking of this vision, Ambrose himself, also its lover and longer, says: 'God is not seen in a place', as at the oak of Mamre, as on Mount Sinai, 'but by a pure heart'; and he continues, knowing what he desires and what he burns for and what he hopes: 'Nor is God sought with bodily eyes', with which he showed himself to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and others in this world, 'nor is he circumscribed by sight', on account of what was said: You shall see my back parts, 'nor is he held by touch', as when he even wrestled with Jacob, 'nor is he heard by speech', as he was heard not only by so many saints but even by the devil, 'nor is he perceived by walking', as once when he walked in paradise toward evening.

passages.original: ideo, cum dixisset: \'Nec corporalibus oculis deus quaeritur nec circumscribitur uisu nec tactu tenetur\', addidit etiam: \'Nec auditur affatu\', ut, si possumus, unigenitum filium, qui est in sinu patris, sic intellegamus narrantem, quo modo et uerbum est non sonus auribus instrepens sed imago mentibus innotescens, ut illic interna et ineffabili luce clarescat, quod dictum est: Qui me uidit, uidit et patrem, quod hic Philippo dicebatur, quando uidebat et non uidebat sequitur enim huius uisionis eximius concupitor Ambrosius dicens:
passages.english: Therefore, when he had said, 'God is not sought with bodily eyes, nor circumscribed by sight, nor held by touch', he also added, 'nor is he heard by speech', so that, if we can, we may understand the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, as declaring [him] in such a way as he is also the Word, not a sound resounding in the ears but an image making itself known to minds, so that there, in an inward and ineffable light, what was said may become clear: 'He who has seen me has seen the Father also', which was said here to Philip when he saw and did not see. For Ambrose, that outstanding lover of this vision, continues, saying:

passages.original: quocirca id, quod scriptum est: Deum nemo uidit umquam, et: Lucem habitat inaccessibilem, quem nemo hominum uidit nec uidere potest, et: Beati mundo corde, quia ipsi deum uidebunt, et quicquid aliud ex illis sanctis libris commemoraui, firmius credis quam id, quod dixit Ambrosius: (Nec in loco deus uidetur nec corporalibus oculis quaeritur nec circumscribitur uisu nec tactu tenetur nec auditur affatu nec sentitur incessu\'. talem quippe esse intellexit uel credidit deum, qui mundo corde conspicitur; hanc autem etiam meam sententiam esse confiteor.
passages.english: Therefore what is written, 'No one has ever seen God', and, 'He dwells in unapproachable light, whom no human being has seen or can see', and, 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God', and whatever else I have cited from those holy books, you believe more firmly than what Ambrose said: 'God is not seen in a place, nor sought with bodily eyes, nor circumscribed by sight, nor held by touch, nor heard by speech, nor perceived by his approach.' For he understood or believed God to be such, he who is beheld by the pure in heart; and I confess that this is also my own view.
passages.notes: 'nec sentitur incessu' is taken as 'nor perceived by his coming/movement'; the sense is not certain.

passages.original: Sanctas autem Hieronymus ait: \'Videre deum, sicuti est, in natura sua oculus hominis non potest, non solum homo nec angeli nec Throni nec Potestates nec Dominationes nec omne nomen, quod nominatur; neque enim creatura potest aspicere creatorem suum\'. his uerbis uir doctissimus satis ostendit, quid etiam de futuro saeculo senserit, quod ad hanc rem adtinet. quantum libet enim oculi corporis nostri mutentur in melius, angelorum oculis aequabuntur.
passages.english: Saint Jerome, moreover, says: 'The eye of man cannot see God as he is in his own nature; and not only man, but neither angels nor Thrones nor Powers nor Dominions nor any name that is named; for a creature cannot look upon its creator.' With these words that most learned man shows clearly enough what he thought also about the world to come, so far as this matter is concerned. For however much the eyes of our body are changed for the better, they will [only] be made equal to the eyes of angels.
passages.notes: 'Sanctas' read as 'Sanctus'.

passages.original: aequalem trinitatis inuisibilitatem scripturarum sanctarum testimoniis et diligentia suae disputationis adseruit instantissime suadens deum non esse uisum nisi adsumptione creaturae, secundum deitatis autem suae proprietatem omnino deum esse inuisibilem, id est patrem et filium et spiritum sanctum, nisi quantum mente ac spiritu nosci potest Gregorius etiam, sanctus episcopus orientalis, apertissime dicit deum natura inuisibilem, quando patribus uisus est sicut Moysi, cum quo facie ad faciem loquebatur, alicuius conspicabilis materiae dispositione adsumpta salua sua inuisibilitate uideri potuisse. hoc est, quod etiam noster dicit Ambrosius et patrem et filium et spiritum sanctum ea specie uideri, quam uoluntas elegerit, non natura formauerit, ut et illud uerum sit, quod deum nemo uidit umquam, quae uox ipsius domini Christi est, et: Quem nemo hominum uidit nec uidere potest, quae uox apostoli, immo eius per apostolum Christi est, et illa non repudientur testimonia scripturarum, quibus deus uisus esse narratur, quia et inuisibilis est per propriam deitatis naturam et, cum uult, uideri potest per adsumptam, sicut placuerit, creaturam.
passages.english: he maintained the equal invisibility of the Trinity by testimonies of the holy Scriptures and by the care of his argument, most urgently persuading [readers] that God has not been seen except by the assumption of a creature, but that according to the property of his deity God is wholly invisible, that is, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, except so far as he can be known by the mind and spirit. Gregory too, a holy bishop of the East, says most plainly that God, invisible by nature, when he was seen by the fathers, as by Moses, with whom he spoke face to face, was able to be seen by taking on an arrangement of some visible matter while his invisibility remained intact. This is what our Ambrose also says: that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are seen in that form which [their] will has chosen, not [their] nature has formed; so that both that is true, that no one has ever seen God, which is the word of the Lord Christ himself, and, 'whom no human being has seen or can see', which is the word of the apostle, or rather of Christ through the apostle; and those testimonies of Scripture in which God is related to have been seen are not rejected, because he is both invisible through the proper nature of his deity and, when he wishes, can be seen through a creature assumed as it pleases [him].
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject (from the preceding context) is Athanasius.

passages.original: quo modo ergo dicitur \'pater uester caelestis\', quibus dicitur cum sitis mali\', nisi quia utrumque ueritas monstrat, quid simus dei bono, quid humano uitio, hoc commendans, illud emendans? merito ait Seneca, qui temporibus apostolorum fuit, cuiu* etiam quaedam ad Paulum apostolum leguntur epistulae: 'Omnes odit, qui malos odit\'. et tamen ideo sunt diligendi mali, ut non sint mali, quem ad modum, non ut permaneant.
passages.english: How then is 'your heavenly Father' said to those to whom it is said, 'though you are evil', unless because the truth shows both: what we are by God's goodness and what by human vice, commending the one and correcting the other? Rightly does Seneca say, who lived in the times of the apostles, and some of whose letters to the apostle Paul are also read: 'He hates all who hates the wicked.' And yet the wicked are to be loved for this reason, that they may not be wicked, just as, not so that they may remain [so],
passages.notes: 'cuiu*' read as 'cuius'. The final clause continues in the following sentence ('the sick are loved so that they may be healed').

passages.original: Est apud Ciceronem in extrema, ut scis, parte quinti Tusculanarum libri locus propter hoc, quod dico. animaduertendus. cum enim de caecitate corporis ageret atque adfirmaret etiam caecum beatum esse posse sapientem, multa dixit, quae per aures percipiendo gauderet, itemque, si surdus esset, ea, quibus oblectaretur, ad oculos transtulit;
passages.english: There is a passage in Cicero, as you know, at the very end of the fifth book of the Tusculans, that deserves notice in view of what I am saying. For when he was treating of blindness of the body and asserting that even a blind wise man can be happy, he mentioned many things in which he could take delight through perceiving them by the ears; and likewise, if he were deaf, he transferred to the eyes the things by which he might be delighted;

passages.original: cuius et illi gratiam mererentur, nisi elati inflatique superbia inaniter conarentur istam uitam beatam sibi ipsi facere, quod solus deus ueraciter cultoribus suis post hanc uitam se largiturum esse promisit. sanior quippe est eiusdem Ciceronis illa sententia, ubi ait: Nam haec quidem uita mors est, quam lamentari possem, si liberet\'. quo modo ergo, si recte lamentatur, beata comprobatur ac non potius, quoniam recte lamentatur, misera esse conuincitur? quare adsuesce, obsecro te, uir bone, beatus esse interim spe, ut sis etiam re, cum pietati perseuerantissimae retribuetur merces felicitatis aeternae.
passages.english: whose grace they too would have merited, had they not, lifted up and puffed with pride, vainly tried to make that happy life for themselves, which God alone has truly promised that he will bestow on his worshippers after this life. For sounder is that saying of the same Cicero, where he says: 'For this life indeed is death, which I could lament if I wished.' How then, if it is rightly lamented, is it proved happy, and is it not rather, since it is rightly lamented, shown to be wretched? Therefore accustom yourself, I beg you, good sir, to be happy meanwhile in hope, so that you may also be so in reality, when the reward of eternal happiness is paid to persevering piety.

passages.original: Cum enim omnis, qui renuntiat huic saeculo, sine dubio renuntiet omnibus, quae sunt eius, ut Christi possit esse discipulus — ipse enim, cum de sumptibus ad turris aedificium necessariis et de bello aduersus regem alterum praeparando similitudines praemisisset, adiunxit sic: Qui non renuntiat omnibus, quae sunt eius, non potest meus discipulus esse —, profecto renuntiat etiam diuitiis suis, si quas habet, aut sic, ut eas omnino non diligens totas distribuat indigentibus et superfluis exoneretur sarcinis, aut sic, ut plus diligens Christum spem ab eis transferat in ipsum atque ita utatur illis, ut facile tribuens et communicans thesaurizet in caelo paratusque sit, quem ad modum parentes et filios et fratres et uxorem, hoc modo et istas relinquere, si talis condicio proposita fuerit, ut nisi dimisso Christo eas habere non possit. nam si aliter huic saeculo renuntiat, quando accedit ad fidei sacramentum, facit, quod de lapsis beatus Cyprianus ingemit dicens: \'Saeculo uerbis solis et non factis renuntiantes\'. de hoc quippe dicitur, cum ueniente temptatione magis ista metuit amittere quam Christum negare: Ecce homo, qui coepit aedificare et non potuit perficere. ipse est etiam, qui, cum adhuc longe esset aduersarius eius, mittit legatos quaerens pacem, id est nondum affligente sed adhuc imminente ac minante temptatione, ut his non careat, quae plus diligit, ad relinquendum Christum negandumque consentit.
passages.english: For since everyone who renounces this world without doubt renounces all that is his, so that he can be a disciple of Christ — for he himself, after first giving the comparisons about the costs needed for building a tower and about preparing for war against another king, added this: 'Whoever does not renounce all that is his cannot be my disciple' — he certainly also renounces his riches, if he has any, either in such a way that, not loving them at all, he distributes them wholly to the needy and is relieved of superfluous burdens, or in such a way that, loving Christ more, he transfers his hope from them to him and so uses them that, giving readily and sharing, he lays up treasure in heaven, and is ready, just as [he would leave] parents and children and brothers and wife, in the same way to leave these too, if such a condition were set before him that he could not have them except by abandoning Christ. For if he renounces this world otherwise when he comes to the sacrament of faith, he does what blessed Cyprian laments concerning the lapsed, saying: 'Renouncing the world by words alone and not by deeds.' Of such a man indeed it is said, when on the coming of temptation he fears to lose these things more than to deny Christ: 'Behold the man who began to build and could not finish.' He is also the one who, while his adversary is still far off, sends envoys seeking peace, that is, while temptation is not yet afflicting but still impending and threatening, he consents to abandon and deny Christ so as not to lose those things which he loves more.

passages.original: Tandem ex Africa uestrae litteras unanimitatis accepi et non me paenitet inpudentiae, qua tacentibus uobis epistulas meas frequenter ingessi, ut rescriptum mererer et uos esse sospites non aliis nuntiantibus sed uestro potissimum sermone cognoscerem. super animae statu memini uestrae quaestiunculae, immo maximae ecclesiasticae quaestionis, utrum lapsa de caelo sit, ut Pythagoras philosophus omnesque Platonici et Origenes putant, an anippoia dei substantiae, ut Stoici, Manichaeus et Hispana Priscilliani haeresis suspicantur, an in thesauro habeantur dei olim conditae. ut quidam ecclesiastici stulta persuasione confidunt, an cotidie a deo fiant et mittantur in corpora secundum illud, quod in euangelio scriptum est: Pater meus usque modo operatur et ego operor, an certe ex traduce, ut Tertullianus, Apollinaris et maxima pars occidentalium autumat, ut quo modo corpus ex corpore sic anima nascatur ex anima et simili cum brutis animantibus condicione subsistat. super quo quid mihi uideretur, in opusculis contra Rutinum olim scripsisse me noui aduersus eum libellum.
passages.english: At last I have received a letter from Africa from your unanimity, and I do not regret the impudence with which, while you kept silent, I frequently thrust my letters upon you, so that I might earn a reply and learn that you were safe not from others' reports but above all from your own words. I remember your little question about the state of the soul — or rather a very great question of the Church: whether it has fallen from heaven, as the philosopher Pythagoras and all the Platonists and Origen think; or is an emanation of God's substance, as the Stoics, Manichaeus and the Spanish heresy of Priscillian suppose; or whether souls are kept in God's treasury, created long ago, as some churchmen trust with foolish conviction; or whether they are made daily by God and sent into bodies, according to what is written in the Gospel, 'My Father is working until now, and I am working'; or indeed [come] by transmission, as Tertullian, Apollinaris and the greater part of the Westerners hold, so that as body is born from body, so soul from soul, and it subsists in a condition like that of brute animals. What my view on this was, I know I wrote long ago in my short works against Rufinus, against that pamphlet
passages.notes: 'anippoia' is evidently a corrupt Greek word, probably 'aporrhoia' (emanation). 'Rutinum' read as 'Rufinum'. This letter is by Jerome to Augustine's correspondents, preserved among Augustine's letters.

passages.original: Ezechielis uolumen olim adgredi uolui et sponsionem creberrimam studiosis lectoribus reddere, sed in ipso dictandi exordio ita animus meus occidentalium prouinciarum et maxime urbis Romae uastatione confusus est, ut iuxta uulgare prouerbium proprium quoque ignorarem uocabulum, diuque tacui sciens tempus esse lacrimarum. hoc autem anno, cum tres explicassem libros, subitus impetus barbarorum, de quibus tuus dicit Vergilius: \'Lateque uagantes Barcaei\' et sancta scriptura de Ismahel: Contra faciem omnium fratrum s u o r u u h a b i t a b i t, sic Aegypti limitem, Palaestinae, Phoenices, Syriae percucurrit ad instar torrentis cuncta secum trahens, ut uix manus eorum misericordia Christi potuerimus euadere.
passages.english: I long ago wished to undertake the volume of Ezekiel and fulfil my oft-repeated promise to studious readers, but at the very outset of dictating my mind was so confounded by the devastation of the western provinces and above all of the city of Rome that, as the common proverb has it, I did not even know my own name; and I was long silent, knowing that it was a time for tears. This year, however, when I had completed three books, a sudden onrush of barbarians — of whom your Virgil says, 'and the far-roaming Barcaei', and holy Scripture says of Ishmael, 'He shall dwell over against the face of all his brothers' — so overran the borders of Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia and Syria, like a torrent sweeping everything with it, that by the mercy of Christ we were barely able to escape their hands.
passages.notes: 's u o r u u h a b i t a b i t' read as 'suorum habitabit'. Letter of Jerome.

passages.original: Quod propterea commemorauimus, quoniam quidam etiam apud uos uel in uestra potius ciuitate. si tamen uerum est, quod audiuimus, tanta pro isto errore obstinatione nituntur, st dicant facilius esse, ut etiam Pelagium deserant atque contemnant, qui haec sentientes anathemauit, quam ut ab huius sententiae, sicut eis uidetur, ueritate discedant. si autem cedunt sedi apostolicae uel potius ipsi magistro et domino apostolorum qui dicit non habituros uitam in semet ipsis, nisi manducauerint carnem filii hominis et biberint sanguinem, quod nisi baptizati non utique possunt.
passages.english: We have mentioned this because certain people even among you, or rather in your city, if what we have heard is true, strive for this error with such obstinacy that they say it would be easier for them even to desert and despise Pelagius, who anathematized those holding these views, than to depart from what seems to them the truth of this opinion. But if they yield to the apostolic see, or rather to the very master and lord of the apostles, who says that they will not have life in themselves unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, which they certainly cannot do unless baptized,
passages.notes: 'st' read as 'ut'. The final sentence is a protasis completed in the following context ('surely they will at some point admit...').

passages.original: Ubi est ergo: Quid est homo, nisi quod memor es eius? ubi postremo illa testimonia. quae Hierosolymitanae antistes ecclesiae, sicut in eisdem gestis legitur. ipsi Pelagio se dixisse commemorat. cum ad eum perlatum esset. quod sine gratia dei diceret absque peccato esse hominem posse? haec sunt enim ab illo dicta tria testimonia ualde magna contra huius modi impiam praesumptionem, quod apostolus ait: Plus omnibus illis laboraui. non ego autem sed gratia dei mecum, et: Non uolentis neque currentis sed miserentis est dei, et: Nisi dominus aedificauerit domum in uanum laborauerunt aedificantes eam. quo modo ergo, quod deus iubet, sine diuinitus ipsius uel difficile impletur, cum. si dominus non aedificet, in uanum aedificans laborasse dicatur neque scriptum sit ceat quidem uolentis atque currentis, facilius autem miserentis est dei, sed scriptum sit: Non uolentis neque currentis sed miserentis est dei, non quia nulla est hominis uoluntas atque cursus, sed quia nihil potest, nisi misereatur deus, nec apostolus dixerit \'et ego\', sed dixerit: Non ego antem sed gratia dei mecum, non quia ipse nihil boni agebat, sed quia nihil ageret, si illa non adiuuaret?
passages.english: Where then is: 'What is man, that you are mindful of him?' Where, finally, are those testimonies which the bishop of the church of Jerusalem, as is read in the same proceedings, recalls that he quoted to Pelagius himself when it had been reported to him that [Pelagius] said that a man could be without sin without the grace of God? For these are the three very weighty testimonies he cited against this kind of impious presumption: that the apostle says, 'I laboured more than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God with me'; and 'It is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy'; and 'Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have laboured in vain.' How then is what God commands fulfilled even with difficulty without his divine [help], when it is said that if the Lord does not build, the builder has laboured in vain; and when it is not written that it is indeed of him who wills and runs, but more easily of God who shows mercy, but it is written, 'It is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy'—not because there is no will or running on man's part, but because it can do nothing unless God shows mercy; and when the apostle did not say 'and I', but said, 'Yet not I, but the grace of God with me'—not because he himself did nothing good, but because he would do nothing if it did not help him?
passages.notes: 'sine diuinitus ipsius' appears to lack a noun (e.g. 'adiutorio', help); 'ceat' is corrupt, perhaps for 'licet' or 'esse'. 'antem' read as 'autem'.

passages.original: non uult eam in domino gloriari, sed sic gloriari, quasi non acceperit. in quo libro quamuis nec ipsius nec tuae reuerentiae nomen expresserit, tamen a matre uirginis, ut ad eam scriberet, a se postulatum esse commemorat. in quadam uero epistula sua idem Pelagius, ubi et nomen suum apertissime ponit nec nomen sacrae uirginis tacet, dicit ad eam se scripsisse et eiusdem sui operis testimonio probare nititur se gratiam dei. quam uel tacere uel negare adseritur, apertissime confiteri. sed utrum ipse sit liber, in quo de spiritalibus diuitiis illa uerba posuit.
passages.english: he does not want her to glory in the Lord, but to glory as though she had not received [it]. In that book, although he expressed neither her name nor that of your reverence, he nevertheless mentions that he was asked by the virgin's mother to write to her. But in a certain letter of his, where the same Pelagius sets down his own name quite openly and does not keep silent the name of the holy virgin, he says that he wrote to her, and tries to prove by the testimony of that same work of his that he most openly confesses the grace of God, which he is alleged either to pass over in silence or to deny. But whether this is the very book in which he set down those words about spiritual riches,
passages.notes: The sentence continues in the following context ('or whether it has reached your holiness, we ask you to inform us').

passages.original: Si autem non inueneris, qua re uel quo modo fiant animae infantium peccatrices et nihil in se ipsis habentes malitiae a quo cogantur ex Adam trahere, unde damnentur, cum eas credas non ex illa prima peccatrice propagatas sed nouas atque insontes includi carne peccati, nec sic iam temere in aliam sententiam tua deflectatur assensio, ut eas ex illa una credas propagando traduci, ne forte alius inuenire possit. quod ipse non possis, aut aliquando inuenias, quod nunc non potueris. nam et illi. qui animas ex una propagari adserunt, quam deus homini primo dedit, atque ita eas ex parentibus trahi dicunt, si Tertulliani opinionem sequuntur, profecto eas non spiritus sed corpora esse contendunt et corpulentis seminibus exoriri. quo peruersius quid dici potest? neque hoc Tertullianum somniasse mirandum est. qui etiam ipsum creatorem deum non esse nisi corpus opinatur.
passages.english: But if you do not find for what reason or in what way the souls of infants become sinful, and, though they have no wickedness in themselves, by what they are compelled to draw from Adam that for which they are condemned, since you believe that they are not propagated from that first sinful [soul] but are enclosed, new and innocent, in the flesh of sin, let your assent not on that account rashly turn aside to the other opinion, so that you believe they are transmitted by propagation from that one [soul], lest perhaps another may be able to find what you yourself cannot, or you may at some time find what you have not been able to now. For those too who assert that souls are propagated from the one which God gave to the first man, and so say that they are drawn from the parents, if they follow the opinion of Tertullian, certainly contend that they are not spirits but bodies, and arise from bodily seeds. What could be said more perversely than that? Nor is it to be wondered at that Tertullian dreamed this, since he holds that even God the creator himself is nothing but a body.
passages.notes: The printed punctuation ('possit. quod ipse', 'illi. qui') is faulty; translated as continuous clauses.

passages.original: Sed sine isto modo intellegenda sit dierum illa breuiatio sine quod ad paucitatem redigerentur sine quod cursu solis celeriore breuiarentur — non enim desunt, qui et hoc existiment, ita scilicet dictos breuiores dies futuros, sicut fuit longior dies orante Iesu Naue —, tamen Lucas euangelista et hanc dierum breuiationem et abominationem desolationis, quae duo ipse non dixit, sed Matthaeus Marcusque dixerunt, ad euersionem Hierusalem docuit pertinere alia cum eis dicens \' apertius de hac eadem re, quae illi posuerunt obscurius. nam Iosephus, qui Iudaicam scripsit historiam, talia mala dicit illi populo tunc accidisse, ut uix credibilia uideantur. unde non inmerito dictum est talem tribulationem nec fuisse a creaturae initio nec futuram. sed etsi tempore Antichristi talis aut maior forsitan erit, intellegendum est de illo populo dictum.
passages.english: But whether that shortening of the days is to be understood in this way, or as meaning that they would be reduced to a small number, or that they would be shortened by a swifter course of the sun (for there are those who think this too, namely that the days were said to be going to be shorter in the way that the day was longer when Joshua son of Nun prayed), nevertheless Luke the evangelist taught that both this shortening of the days and the abomination of desolation, two things which he himself did not mention but Matthew and Mark did, pertain to the overthrow of Jerusalem, saying other things along with them more openly about this same matter, which they set down more obscurely. For Josephus, who wrote the Jewish history, says that such evils befell that people at that time that they seem scarcely credible. Hence it was not without reason said that such tribulation had not been from the beginning of creation, nor would be. But even if in the time of Antichrist there will perhaps be such or greater, it must be understood as said of that people,
passages.notes: 'sine ... sine ... sine' read as 'siue ... siue ... siue' (scanning error). A stray mark after 'dicens' omitted.

passages.original: Dudum quidem fuerat constitutum, ut Pelagius atque Caelestius, infandi dogmatis repertores, ab urbe Roma uelut quaedam catholicae unitatis contagia pellerentur, ne ignorantium mentes scaeua persuasione peruerterent. in quo secuta est clementia nostra iudicium sanctitatis tuae.
passages.english: It had indeed been decreed some time ago that Pelagius and Caelestius, the inventors of an unspeakable doctrine, should be driven from the city of Rome as being a kind of infection of catholic unity, lest they pervert the minds of the ignorant by their perverse persuasion. In this our clemency followed the judgement of your holiness.
passages.notes: This is an imperial rescript preserved among Augustine's letters.

passages.original: Philastrius quidam, Brixensis episcopus, quem cum sancto Ambrosio Mediolani etiam ipse uidi, scripsit hinc librum nec illas haereses praetermittens, quae in populo Iudaeo fuerunt ante domini aduentum, easque XX et VIII commemorauit et post domini aduentum CXX et VIII. scripsit hinc etiam Graece episcopus Cyprius Epiphanius in doctrina catholicae fidei laudabiliter diffamatus.
passages.english: A certain Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, whom I myself also saw with Saint Ambrose at Milan, wrote a book on this, not passing over even those heresies which existed among the Jewish people before the Lord's coming, and he recorded twenty-eight of these, and after the Lord's coming one hundred and twenty-eight. Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, also wrote on this in Greek, a man widely and praiseworthily renowned in the teaching of the catholic faith.
passages.notes: 'diffamatus' here in the positive sense 'spread abroad, renowned'.

passages.original: et hoc non solum aliorum catholicorum testimoniis sed etiam sanctitatis tuae disputatione antiquiore se probare testantur, ubi tamen eandem gratiam non minore ueritatis perspicuitate docueris, ut est illud, quod dixit sanctitas tua in quaestione contra Porphyrium de tempore Christianae religionis: Tunc uoluisse hominibus apparere Christum et apud eos praedicari doctrinam suam, quando sciebat et ubi sciebat esse, qui in eum fuerant credituri uel illud de libro in epistula ad Romanos: \'Dicis itaque mihi: Quid adhuc conqueritur?nam uoluntati eius quis resistit?
passages.english: and they declare that they prove this not only by the testimonies of other catholics but also by an earlier discussion of Your Holiness, where nevertheless you had taught that same grace with no less clarity of truth, such as that which Your Holiness said in the question against Porphyry on the time of the Christian religion: that Christ willed to appear to men and to have his teaching preached among them at the time when he knew, and where he knew, there were those who would believe in him; or that from the book on the Epistle to the Romans: 'You say to me, then: Why does he still find fault? For who resists his will?

passages.original: uiderint ergo, quo fine qua intentione illud dixisse crediderint uel ipse qua dixerit. erat enim secundum hoc saeculum uir magnificus. nam etiam cum ei dictum fuisset: \'Quid igitur nosti?\' \'Rem publicam\', inquit, \'ex parua magnam facere. ego autem, quod ait Ennius: (Omnes mortales sese laudari exoptant), partim puto adprobandum partim cauendum. ut enim appetenda est ueritas, quae procul dubio est, etiam si non laudetur, sola laudabilis. sic ea, quae facile subrepit, uanitas in hominum laude fugienda est: haec est autem, cam uel ipsa bona.
passages.english: Let them consider, then, with what aim and intention they believe he said that, or with what [intention] he himself said it. For by the standards of this world he was a great man. For when he had also been asked, 'What then do you know?', he said, 'How to make a small state great.' As for me, regarding what Ennius says, 'All mortals long to be praised', I think it is partly to be approved and partly to be guarded against. For just as truth is to be sought, which beyond doubt, even if it is not praised, is alone praiseworthy, so that vanity which easily creeps in through human praise is to be shunned; and this is [vanity], when even the good things themselves
passages.notes: 'cam' read as 'cum'. The sentence continues into the following context.

passages.original: quae laudatione digna sunt, non putantur habenda, nisi laudetur ab hominibus homo. uel ea quoque uult in se multum quisque laudari, quae aut exigua laude aut etiam uituperatione digniora sunt. unde Horatius Ennio uigilantior ait: Laudis amore tumes? sunt certa piacula, quae te ter pure lecto poterunt recreare libello.
passages.english: things that are worthy of praise are not thought to be possessed unless a man is praised by men. Or else each person wishes to be much praised even for those things in himself which deserve either slight praise or even rather blame. Hence Horace, more watchful than Ennius, says: 'Are you swelling with love of praise? There are sure expiations which can restore you, once the little book has been purely read three times.'
passages.notes: Sentence begins mid-thought; the preceding context appears to be partly corrupt ('cam' probably 'cum').

passages.original: Abripui uel potius subripui et quodam modo furatus sum memet ipsum multis occupationibus meis. ut tibi scriberem antiquissimo amico, quem tamen non habebam, quam diu in Christo non tenebam. nosti quippe, ut definierit amicitiam \'Romani\', ut ait quidam, \'maximus auctor Tullius eloquii\'. dixit enim et uerissime dixit: \'Amicitia est rerum humanarum et diuinarum cum beniuolentia et caritate consensio\'. tu autem, mi carissime, aliquando mihi consentiebas in rebus humanis, cum eis more uulgi frui cuperem, et milii ad ea capessenda, quorum me paenitet.
passages.english: I have snatched away, or rather stolen away, and in a certain way filched myself from my many occupations, so as to write to you, my oldest friend, whom nevertheless I did not have as long as I did not hold you in Christ. For you know how 'Tullius, the greatest author of Roman eloquence', as someone says, defined friendship. For he said, and said most truly: 'Friendship is agreement on things human and divine, with goodwill and affection.' But you, my dearest, once agreed with me in human things, when I desired to enjoy them in the manner of the crowd, and toward the pursuit of those things of which I now repent,
passages.notes: 'milii' read as 'mihi'. The sentence continues into the following context.
